questions.stem: A training coordinator asks Claude for a new-hire onboarding checklist covering about 40 steps across IT setup, HR paperwork and team introductions. She will refine it with Claude over several rounds this week, and her team will reuse and update it every quarter. Which output format is MOST appropriate?

options.text: An inline bulleted list in the chat, which she can scroll back to and copy from whenever the team needs it.
An interactive dashboard artifact that tracks every new hire's completion progress with charts, filters and live status counters.
An artifact holding the checklist as a self-contained document she can keep iterating on, reuse and later share.
A short inline summary of the main onboarding phases, leaving the detailed steps for managers to fill in.

questions.explanation: The checklist is substantial, self-contained, will be revised over several rounds and reused every quarter — exactly the signals for an **artifact**: significant, self-contained content meant to be edited, iterated on, and reused or shared outside the conversation. Inline output scrolls away; an artifact gives her one living version to keep improving.

whyWrong.A: A 40-step list left inline scrolls away, is awkward to revise round after round, and is not a clean reusable deliverable.
whyWrong.B: A tracking dashboard is the most impressive option, but nobody asked for progress tracking. It adds complexity without serving the actual need: a reusable checklist.
whyWrong.D: Dropping the detail fails the request. The team needs the full set of steps, not a phase outline.

questions.mindset: Pick the format by what happens next: edit, reuse and share point to an artifact.

questions.stem: Halfway through writing an email, a project manager asks Claude: 'In Outlook, what's the practical difference between CC and BCC when I reply to a client group?' He just wants to understand it quickly and get back to his email. What is the BEST format for Claude's answer?

options.text: An artifact containing a one-page reference guide on email etiquette that he can save and share with his team later.
A short inline answer in the chat explaining the difference and when each one fits his client reply.
A comparison table artifact listing every Outlook recipient field with columns for visibility, privacy and reply behavior across common cases.
A Word document explaining CC and BCC that he can attach to the project folder for future reference.

questions.explanation: This is a quick, read-once question in the middle of a task. An **inline answer** is fastest and fits the need. Artifacts and files make sense for substantial content that will be edited, reused or shared, which does not describe a two-sentence explanation.

whyWrong.A: A reference guide is more than he asked for and slows him down. Nothing suggests he wants to keep or share it.
whyWrong.C: A full table of every recipient field over-engineers a simple question and buries the one distinction he needs.
whyWrong.D: Creating a file for a one-off explanation adds overhead with no benefit to the task in front of him.

questions.mindset: Don't over-engineer: a quick, read-once answer belongs inline.

questions.scenario: An event planner has 200 RSVP emails for a conference dinner. Guests wrote their meal needs in free text ('veggie please', 'no nuts — severe allergy', 'whatever is fine'). The caterer's ordering system imports a spreadsheet with one row per guest.
questions.stem: She wants Claude to turn the RSVPs into something she can load into the caterer's system with the fewest manual fixes. Which request is MOST effective?

options.text: Ask Claude for a friendly narrative summary of the guests' dietary needs that she can forward to the caterer as context.
Ask Claude to count how many guests fall into each dietary category and report the totals inline for her ordering call.
Ask Claude to put the RSVPs into an artifact so the full text of every email is collected in one place for the caterer.
Ask for one row per guest with fixed columns (name, meal type from a set list, allergies, notes) and 'unclear' where unsure.

questions.explanation: The output is going into another tool, so it should be **structured data** that matches the import: one row per guest, fixed columns, and a fixed set of allowed values. Telling Claude to write 'unclear' instead of guessing makes ambiguous answers visible, so she can follow up. That matters a lot for something like a severe allergy.

whyWrong.A: Prose can't be imported and forces someone to retype every guest's needs, which invites errors.
whyWrong.B: Totals help with ordering, but the caterer's system needs per-guest rows, and counts hide which guest has which allergy.
whyWrong.C: Collecting raw emails in an artifact organizes nothing. The free text still has to be turned into rows by hand.

questions.mindset: When the output feeds another tool, ask for fixed columns and allowed values, and flag uncertainty instead of guessing.

questions.stem: A chief of staff needs a 10-slide quarterly update for the board. The finance team will edit the figures directly in PowerPoint, and the deck must go out in the company's standard slide format. File creation is enabled in her Claude workspace. Which approach BEST fits this deliverable?

options.text: Have Claude create a .pptx file from the source figures, then have finance edit it and check every number before it goes out.
Have Claude build an interactive web dashboard artifact of the quarter's results and send the board a link to it.
Have Claude write all ten slides as inline text in the chat so she can copy each section into PowerPoint by hand.
Have Claude produce a polished long-form written report of the quarter instead, since that gives the board more detail than slides.

questions.explanation: The downstream need is an **editable file in the company's standard slide format** that finance will work on in PowerPoint. With file creation available in the workspace, Claude can produce the .pptx directly instead of her rebuilding it by hand. A polished file isn't automatically an accurate one, though, so the figures still need checking against the source before the board sees them.

whyWrong.B: A dashboard is impressive but ignores the stated requirement: finance edits in PowerPoint and the board expects the standard deck.
whyWrong.C: Copying ten slides by hand is slow and error-prone when a file can be produced directly.
whyWrong.D: This swaps the requested deliverable for a different one. The board and finance process are built around slides.

questions.mindset: Match the format to how others will work with it, and remember that polish doesn't replace checking.

questions.stem: A strategy consultant used Claude to synthesize 12 analyst reports into a market brief for a client's executive team. The draft is 9 pages long. Findings drawn from the reports are mixed in with Claude's own predictions, and the executives have said they'll spend about five minutes on it. Which TWO changes would MOST improve the brief? Choose TWO.

options.text: Add the remaining minor findings from the reports so the executives can see that nothing in the source material was left out.
Open with a short summary of the three findings that matter most for the client's decision, with supporting detail after it.
Turn the brief into an interactive artifact with charts and expandable sections so the executives can explore the detail themselves.
Ask Claude to rate its confidence in each section from 1 to 10 and quietly drop every section that scores below seven.
Label each point as either a finding from a named report or Claude's interpretation, so readers know which is which.

questions.explanation: Two problems: it's too long for five minutes, and sourced facts are mixed with AI inference. **Curating** fixes the first: lead with what matters most and put the detail after it. **Labeling** fixes the second: separating findings from named reports from Claude's interpretation lets executives weigh each point and makes the brief far easier to verify.

whyWrong.A: Adding more content makes the length problem worse. Volume isn't thoroughness.
whyWrong.C: A new visual container doesn't fix the substance. The brief is still unprioritized and still mixes facts with opinion.
whyWrong.D: Claude's self-rated confidence isn't evidence, and silently dropping sections hides decisions from the reader.

questions.mindset: Curate and label: lead with what matters, and keep source facts apart from AI interpretation.

questions.scenario: A customer experience lead asks Claude to organize 400 product complaints from the last quarter into themes for a leadership review. Claude returns five themes ranked by frequency: delivery delays (140), packaging (95), app login (80), billing (60) and 'Other' (25). While spot-checking, she finds that 'Other' includes two reports of a kettle base overheating and scorching a countertop.
questions.stem: What should she do with Claude's grouping before the review?

options.text: Keep the grouping unchanged, since two reports out of 400 are statistically minor and the review should focus on the biggest themes.
Ask Claude to recheck its grouping of the 'Other' bucket and accept its answer about whether the two reports should move.
Pull the overheating reports into their own flagged safety item at the top, and rank by severity as well as frequency.
Ask Claude to split all 400 complaints into twenty smaller themes so that every unusual issue gets its own named category.

questions.explanation: Grouping by frequency can bury a **critical outlier**. Two possible fire-risk reports matter more than 95 packaging complaints, so they need to be visible and escalated. Ranking should match the decision. For a leadership review, severity and safety come alongside volume.

whyWrong.A: Low count isn't low importance. Hiding a possible safety issue in 'Other' is exactly the curation failure to avoid.
whyWrong.B: Asking Claude to recheck itself isn't independent judgment. She has already found the problem and owns the decision.
whyWrong.D: Twenty themes makes the review harder to read and still doesn't rank by severity. The safety issue would just become one of many rows.

questions.mindset: Curation is your judgment: never let grouping or frequency ranking hide a high-severity outlier.

questions.stem: An HR generalist built a benefits FAQ as an artifact with Claude. While drafting, she pasted in a spreadsheet of salary bands and asked Claude to add a section on pay. Now she wants to make the FAQ available to all 300 employees. Which statement BEST describes what she should do?

options.text: Nothing extra. The artifact is already visible to everyone in her organization, so employees can open it from her workspace.
Review the full artifact and remove or approve the pay-band content before publishing, since it stays private until she does.
Publish it right away, because published artifacts are read-only and employees cannot copy or build on the content in any way.
Add a note at the top saying the FAQ was AI-generated, which covers any sensitive details that ended up in the text.

questions.explanation: Artifacts **start private to the creator**, and publishing is what makes them available to others. That publishing step is the natural checkpoint to confirm the content matches the audience. Salary bands may not be meant for all staff, so she should review the whole artifact and remove or get approval for that section before making it available. Published artifacts can also be viewed and built on by others, so she can't count on the content staying contained afterward.

whyWrong.A: Artifacts aren't visible to everyone by default. They start private.
whyWrong.C: Others can view published artifacts and build on them, so 'read-only' gives no protection. Publishing first and checking later is backwards.
whyWrong.D: A disclaimer doesn't remove sensitive content. Labeling isn't the same as curating for the audience.

questions.mindset: Before you share a format, curate its content for the audience. Artifacts start private, so publishing is a deliberate decision.

questions.stem: A school's curriculum lead must show the governing board how the proposed homework policy differs from the current one. Both policies are about four pages long, and board members want to see quickly what changes for students and teachers. Which output should she ask Claude for?

options.text: A table with one row per policy area showing current rule, proposed rule and what changes, each checked against both documents.
A full rewrite of the proposed policy in plain language, so board members can read the new version from start to finish.
A narrative essay walking through the history of the homework policy and the reasoning behind each of the proposed changes.
Both full policies pasted side by side in one long artifact so that board members can compare them line by line themselves.

questions.explanation: The board's task is **comparison**, so a **structured table** with one row per policy area lets them see each difference at a glance. Because every row maps to a specific section, it's also easy to check each entry against both source documents before it goes to the board.

whyWrong.B: A plain-language rewrite shows only the new policy. The board would still have to find the differences themselves.
whyWrong.C: Prose makes side-by-side comparison hard and adds background the board didn't ask for.
whyWrong.D: This organizes nothing. The comparison work is just handed to the readers.

questions.mindset: When readers need to compare, give them structure: rows they can scan and verify.

questions.scenario: Every Friday, a program manager pastes her team's meeting notes into a Claude Project and asks for a status update, which she copies into a shared tracking spreadsheet. Each week the output comes back in a different shape: sometimes a paragraph, sometimes bullets, with statuses written as 'on track', 'green' or 'fine'. Cleaning it up takes her 30 minutes.
questions.stem: Which TWO changes would MOST reliably make the weekly output paste cleanly into the tracker? Choose TWO.

options.text: Add the exact columns, their order and the allowed status values (for example On track / At risk / Blocked) to the Project instructions.
Add a line to the Project instructions asking Claude to please try to be more consistent than it was in previous weeks.
Switch to the most capable model available, since a stronger model will settle on one output format without being told.
Include a correctly filled example row in the Project instructions so Claude can see exactly what a finished entry looks like.
Ask for each week's update as a new artifact so the different shapes are at least kept in separate, tidy documents.

questions.explanation: Consistent structured output comes from **specifying the format precisely** (columns, order, allowed values) and **showing an example** of the finished output. Putting both in the Project instructions applies them every week without retyping. The output then matches the tracker, so her cleanup time disappears.

whyWrong.B: 'Be more consistent' doesn't say what consistent looks like, so Claude still has to guess the format.
whyWrong.C: A more capable model can't guess a format that was never specified. This raises cost without fixing the cause.
whyWrong.E: Putting it in an artifact changes the container, not the structure. The shapes would still vary from week to week.

questions.mindset: Specify the structure and show an example; don't hope for consistency.

questions.stem: A grants officer has spent an afternoon revising a 6-page funding proposal with Claude. Each revision comes back as another full inline reply, and she's now unsure which reply holds the latest wording of the budget justification. What is the BEST change to how she works with Claude on the proposal?

options.text: Keep working inline, but ask Claude at the end to list which reply contains the most recent version of each section.
Start a fresh chat for each section of the proposal so that every conversation holds only one part of the document.
Copy each inline reply into a separate numbered document on her computer after each round of revisions as a backup.
Move the proposal into an artifact so that each revision updates one self-contained document that she can keep iterating on.

questions.explanation: A long document under active revision is exactly what an **artifact** is for: substantial, self-contained content you edit and iterate on. Revisions then land in one place instead of being scattered across many chat replies. That lowers the risk of sending an outdated budget justification.

whyWrong.A: This relies on Claude to rebuild the version history from memory of the chat, which may be wrong, and it leaves the root problem in place.
whyWrong.B: Splitting the document across chats breaks its consistency and makes the final assembly harder.
whyWrong.C: Manual copies add work and still leave her matching versions by hand.

questions.mindset: Content you keep revising belongs in one living document, not scattered across chat replies.

questions.stem: A finance operations manager keeps answering the same staff question: 'How much will I be reimbursed for this trip?' The answer depends on distance, nights away and meal allowances set out in the travel policy. She wants a simple tool staff can use themselves, and she has no developer support. Which approach is MOST appropriate?

options.text: Ask Claude for an inline explanation of the reimbursement formula and paste it into the staff handbook for people to work out themselves.
Build a small interactive calculator artifact from the policy rules, test it against cases with known answers, then share it.
Ask the IT department to scope a custom reimbursement application, since any reliable calculation tool needs a full software project.
Build the calculator artifact and share it right away, because Claude built it from the policy text and will get the rates right.

questions.explanation: Artifacts can be small **interactive tools**, which suits a self-service calculator that a non-developer can build from the policy. Because it produces money figures that staff will rely on, she should **test it on cases with known answers** before sharing it — a wrong rate or rounding rule would otherwise propagate to every claim.

whyWrong.A: Staff would still have to work out the calculation themselves, which is the problem she's trying to remove.
whyWrong.C: This is over-engineered for a simple, policy-driven calculator that an artifact can handle.
whyWrong.D: Being built from the policy isn't verification. A wrong rate or rounding rule would spread to every claim.

questions.mindset: Use the lightest format that does the job, and test anything that produces numbers people will rely on.

questions.scenario: A marketing lead asked Claude to brainstorm names for a new savings product and got 25 options. She has 10 minutes on the brand committee's agenda. The committee's criteria are: under three syllables, no claims about guaranteed returns, and works in both English and Spanish.
questions.stem: Which TWO steps would BEST prepare what she brings to the committee? Choose TWO.

options.text: Present all 25 names, because giving the committee the widest possible choice is more respectful of their final decision-making role.
Ask Claude to generate 50 more names first, so that the final shortlist is drawn from a larger and more varied pool.
Have Claude filter the full list against the committee's three criteria and shortlist three finalists, each with a one-line rationale.
Have Claude format all 25 names as a colorful slide so the committee can scan them more quickly during the meeting.
Ask Claude to list the names it excluded and the criterion each one failed, so she can check the cuts were sound.

questions.explanation: Good **curation** means filtering against the criteria that actually matter, ranking, and leading with a short, justified shortlist. Asking for the excluded names and reasons keeps the filtering transparent: she can catch a strong name that was cut by mistake (for example, a syllable miscount) before the committee sees only three.

whyWrong.A: Twenty-five unfiltered names won't fit in a 10-minute slot and pass on work the committee expects her to do.
whyWrong.B: More volume makes the curation problem bigger and doesn't apply the criteria.
whyWrong.D: Better visuals don't change the substance. The list is still unfiltered.

questions.mindset: Curate down to what the decision-maker needs, and make the cuts visible so they can be checked.

questions.stem: A paralegal needs the renewal date, notice period and auto-renewal status from 60 supplier contracts, collected in one table that the legal team will rely on to avoid missing deadlines. Some contracts are scanned and hard to read. Which instruction to Claude would make the table MOST reliable to check and use?

options.text: For each value, give the clause or page it came from, and write 'not found' instead of estimating when a term is missing or unclear.
Fill every cell in the table, using typical industry terms for any contract where the renewal details are hard to read clearly.
Return the results as a narrative summary grouped by supplier, so the legal team gets fuller context for each contract's terms.
At the end of the table, add an overall confidence score for the whole extraction so the team knows how much to trust it.

questions.explanation: In a structured extraction, a **source column** (clause or page) makes every cell checkable, and an explicit **'not found'** value stops Claude from filling gaps with plausible guesses. With legal deadlines at stake, a blank that's clearly flagged is far safer than a confident wrong date.

whyWrong.B: Filling gaps with typical terms invents data. A table that looks complete would hide exactly the contracts that need human review.
whyWrong.C: Narrative makes 60 contracts hard to scan for deadlines and harder to check row by row.
whyWrong.D: One overall confidence score is self-assessment, not evidence, and it doesn't show which cells are uncertain.

questions.mindset: Build verifiability into the structure: cite the source for each value and allow 'not found' instead of guesses.

questions.stem: A sales operations coordinator asked Claude to turn a messy export of 350 trade-show leads into a clean table matching the columns of the company's CRM import template. The result looks clean: every column is filled in and the formatting is consistent. Before importing, which TWO checks are MOST important? Choose TWO.

options.text: Confirm the table opens cleanly and matches the template's column headings, since a correct structure shows the data is correct.
Check that the row count matches the source and spot-check a sample of rows against the original export, field by field.
Ask Claude to review its own finished table and confirm that every lead was transferred correctly before the import runs.
Look for values that weren't in the source, such as email addresses or job titles that Claude may have filled in or inferred.
Move the table into an artifact first, so the team can view the leads in a more readable layout before importing them.

questions.explanation: Clean structure isn't the same as correct data. **Reconciling the row count and spot-checking rows** against the source catches dropped, duplicated or garbled leads. **Looking for invented values** catches the most dangerous problem in a table where 'every column is filled': plausible emails or titles that never existed would pollute the CRM.

whyWrong.A: Matching the template proves the format, not the content. This is the 'format equals accuracy' trap.
whyWrong.C: Claude grading its own work isn't independent verification and can confidently repeat the same mistakes.
whyWrong.E: Changing the viewing format doesn't check anything.

questions.mindset: A tidy table still needs checking: reconcile it with the source and hunt for filled-in values.

questions.stem: An operations lead wants new hires to understand the purchase-approval process. A request goes to a manager, then to finance if it's over a set amount, then to procurement if a new supplier is involved, and gets returned at any stage if details are missing. Claude's first explanation is four dense paragraphs that new hires keep misreading. What is the BEST next request?

options.text: Ask Claude to add more detail to each paragraph so that every possible path through the approval process is fully explained.
Ask Claude to shorten the explanation to a single paragraph so new hires are more likely to read the whole thing.
Ask Claude to put the four paragraphs into a Word file so the explanation looks more official to the new hires.
Ask Claude for a flowchart artifact showing each step and decision point, then check it against the written approval policy.

questions.explanation: A process with branches and decision points is easier to follow as a **diagram**, and artifacts can be diagrams and flowcharts. The diagram is a reusable reference new hires can come back to. Checking it against the written policy makes sure no threshold or branch was simplified away.

whyWrong.A: More prose makes a branching process harder to follow, not easier.
whyWrong.B: Squeezing four branches into one paragraph is likely to drop conditions and makes misreading more likely.
whyWrong.C: A more official-looking container doesn't change how hard the content is to follow.

questions.mindset: Pick the format that fits the shape of the information: branching processes call for diagrams.
